tldr: The first 3D point tracker capable of tracking all visible points across videos exceeding 1,000 frames. By de-duplicating points in 3D world coordinates and decoding detailed trajectories exclusively for dynamic areas, it scales with physical scene size rather than video duration.
hero_caption: Overview of TrackEverything and its scaling performance on long videos. As shown in the graph on the left, traditional 2D-based methods suffer from a linear explosion of tokens as frames increase, leading to OOM (out of memory). In contrast, the proposed method removes duplicates in 3D space, keeping active tokens nearly constant (a 362x reduction) and enabling all-point tracking across over 1,000 frames on a single GPU with under 40 GB memory.
overview:
For robots to perform tasks in dynamic real-world environments, long-term visual tracking is crucial: knowing where and how every visible object surface in the camera view moves over time. However, conventional point tracking faced a fundamental dilemma. You had to choose between 'sparse trackers' that follow a small set of points over long horizons, or 'dense trackers' that cover the entire screen but exhaust GPU memory after just 48 to 64 frames. As long as video is treated as a sequence of 2D images, the same physical location is repeatedly re-encoded, causing computational and memory costs to explode over time.

The authors returned to a fundamental insight: 'videos are 2D projections of an underlying 3D world.' If you maintain the scene in 3D world coordinates, there is no need to redundantly store static surfaces you have already seen; you only need to add newly revealed surfaces. From this idea, 'TrackEverything' was born. By merging tracking points that reach the same 3D voxel at sliding-window boundaries (de-duplication) and separating the mostly static background from moving objects, it builds an architecture that does not waste compute even on long videos.

In experiments on the standard TAPVid-3D benchmark, TrackEverything outperformed all open-source all-frame dense 3D trackers by more than 20% in APD. Furthermore, while conventional methods run out of memory around 96 frames, TrackEverything effortlessly completes full dense tracking on videos exceeding 1,000 frames. This marks a practical breakthrough toward foundation models for robots operating in dynamic environments.
contributions: Proposed TrackEverything, the first 3D point tracker capable of tracking all visible scene points across videos exceeding 1,000 frames.
Introduced voxelization-based de-duplication at sliding-window boundaries to merge co-located tracks, scaling model complexity with physical scene geometry rather than frame count.

Decoupled tracking into endpoint prediction plus static-versus-dynamic classification, followed by dense trajectory decoding exclusively for dynamic points, and replaced heavy 4D correlation volumes with 3D WAFT feature sampling for dramatic efficiency.
Outperformed all open-source all-frame dense 3D trackers by over 20% APD on short clips on TAPVid-3D, while remaining competitive with state-of-the-art sparse trackers on long sequences.

sections.heading: Why did dense point tracking hit a wall on long horizons?
sections.summary: Because conventional video processing operates on 2D frames, computational cost grew linearly with time even when the scene remained unchanged. This paper introduces a 3D world-coordinate representation that merges redundant observations, scaling with physical scene extent instead of video duration.
sections.details:
Videos are widely used today as inputs for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and robotic policies. However, traditional approaches that process frame-by-frame in 2D pixel space suffer from a fundamental flaw. Even when viewing the exact same static background and objects, new visual tokens are generated each frame, causing compute and memory usage to blow up linearly with video duration.

This issue was especially severe in point tracking. Sparse trackers follow only a handful of query points across long horizons, but they overlook most of the scene. Meanwhile, dense trackers that follow all pixels were either limited to points visible in the first frame or restricted to short clips of only 48 to 64 frames. In other words, tracking all points throughout an entire video—including newly emerging surfaces—was simply impossible.

Here is the key insight: a video is essentially a 2D camera shadow cast by an underlying 3D world. If you maintain the scene in a 3D world coordinate frame from the start, pointing the camera at the same spot generates no new information; the representation only expands when novel, unseen areas come into view.

To realize this idea, TrackEverything introduces three innovations:
- Voxel-based de-duplication: At sliding-window boundaries, points occupying the same 3D location are merged into a single representative track.
- Decoupled endpoint estimation and trajectory decoding: The model first predicts destination positions at the end of the window along with a static-versus-dynamic classification. Expensive detailed trajectory recovery is reserved solely for moving points.
- 3D WAFT (Warp-Aligned Feature Transform): Instead of memory-prohibitive 4D correlation volumes, it relies on ultra-lightweight feature matching via projection and sampling from 3D points onto 2D feature maps.

Together, these techniques enable tracking all visible points across more than 1,000 frames within a single 40 GB GPU.

In the right visualization, the static background is retained as a 3D point cloud, while colored trajectories are drawn exclusively for dynamic objects (horse, dog, robot arm, etc.). As the bar chart on the bottom-left shows, while conventional methods (D4RT, VDPM) all crash with OOM on 1,000+ frame dense tracking, the proposed method runs to completion.

sections.heading: The gap between sparse and dense: limitations of prior tracking methods
sections.summary: Point tracking has been split between sparse trackers following a few query points and dense trackers covering entire grids. Both lines of work were bound to 2D frame redundancy or expensive correlation volumes, falling short of all-point tracking over long videos.
sections.details:
Existing work is broadly split into two paradigms: sparse point tracking and dense point tracking.

### Sparse Point Tracking
Stemming from PIPs and TAP-Vid, recent methods like CoTracker and SpatialTracker track a small set of user-defined query points using sliding windows and iterative refinement. While some recent approaches extend tracking into 3D space, they still retain full-screen image tokens for every frame in their internal representations, making memory consumption grow linearly with time. Furthermore, computing 4D correlation volumes between query features and video features becomes computationally prohibitive as the number of tracked points increases.

### Dense Point Tracking
Dense tracking across the entire screen also required major compromises. 2D methods like DELTA and AllTracker only track points visible in the very first frame, completely ignoring surfaces that emerge later from behind occluders. In 3D, recent methods based on DUSt3R or VGGT (such as Any4D, D4RT, and VDPM) represent surfaces independently per frame. For instance, densely tracking a 200-frame video at $512 \times 512$ resolution would require $10^{10}$ predictions, exhausting GPU memory in short clips of just 48 to 64 frames.

TrackEverything breaks through this computational bottleneck by voxel-merging points at sliding-window boundaries to strip away redundancy and replacing 4D correlation volumes with 3D WAFT.

sections.heading: How it works: de-duplication, endpoint-first, and 3D WAFT
sections.summary: TrackEverything processes 3D feature point clouds derived from the input video and depth in sliding windows of $L=16$ frames. Endpoint positions and dynamic classifications are predicted first, detailed trajectories are refined only for dynamic points, and co-located points are merged via voxelization at window boundaries.
sections.details:
Given a video $\mathbf{I}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times H\times W\times 3}$ and world-coordinate 3D point clouds $\mathbf{P}$ from sensors or pretrained models (such as VGGT-$\Omega$), the model outputs 3D trajectories $\mathbf{X}$, visibility flags $\mathbf{V}$, and static/dynamic flags $\mathbf{S}$ for all scene points.

### 3.1 Encoding
The video is split into non-overlapping sliding windows of $L=16$ frames. Each frame is encoded with a DINOv3-small backbone and a ViT Adapter to produce feature maps at resolution $(H/4, W/4)$. These are paired with 3D point clouds to form world-coordinate tokens, which are first quantized into voxels of size $v$ within each frame and average-pooled. To prevent points from different timestamps from blending prematurely, voxelization at this stage is strictly intra-frame. Concatenating across all frames in the window yields a spatiotemporal feature cloud of size $(N, D)$.

### 3.2 Iterative Refinement
Predicting dense per-frame trajectories for all points at once is wasteful, because most of the real world (floors, walls, furniture) remains static in world coordinates. TrackEverything decomposes this into two stages.

### 3.2.1 Endpoint Refiner
First, the model outputs 3D position residuals $\Delta\mathbf{x}$ at the window target frame ($t_{\mathrm{tgt}}=L-1$), visibility, and static-versus-dynamic classification logits.
- Feature Construction via 3D WAFT: It avoids expensive correlation volumes entirely. The current estimated 3D position is reprojected onto the target frame's 2D feature map to sample feature $\mathbf{g}_{\mathrm{tgt}}$ using bilinear interpolation. This is concatenated with the point's source feature $\mathbf{g}_{\mathrm{src}}$ and point cloud feature $\mathbf{f}_i$. If the source and projected features match, it provides an implicit 'template matching' signal to the model.
- Transformer Self-Attention: Self-attention across the point cloud iteratively refines residuals and classification logits.

### 3.2.2 Trajectory Refiner
Only points classified as 'dynamic' by the endpoint refiner are passed to the trajectory refiner to decode fine-grained trajectories for each frame in the window. After constant-velocity initialization, it alternates temporal self-attention along tracks and cross-attention into scene feature clouds. Omitting track-to-track attention keeps computation lightweight and parallelizable. For points classified as static, trajectory decoding is skipped entirely because they remain in place in world coordinates.

### 3.3 Sliding Window and De-Duplication
This is the most critical component. When a sliding window finishes, all points align at their positions at the window's final timestep. Physically, two different object surfaces cannot occupy the exact same 3D space at the same time. The model voxelizes points at their destination positions and merges co-located points via average pooling (de-duplication). As a result, the representation scales only with the extent of unique 3D physical scene geometry visited, rather than video duration.

captions.F2: Overall architecture of TrackEverything. In the top encoding stage, 2D features and 3D point clouds are combined. The Endpoint Refiner (top right) predicts window-end displacement and static/dynamic masks. In the bottom stage, only dynamic points are routed to the Trajectory Refiner to decode dense trajectories within the window, which are then merged with static points.

sections.heading: Empirical results: overwhelming scalability and accuracy on long videos
sections.summary: Evaluated on TAPVid-3D and PointOdyssey, TrackEverything outperforms existing dense all-frame trackers by over 20% on short clips. It is also the only method capable of sustaining high accuracy on long videos exceeding 900 frames while keeping GPU memory below 30 GB.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Evaluation Setup
Evaluations were conducted on TAPVid-3D, which includes real-world, driving, and studio captures. Performance was evaluated using Average Position Distance (APD), the percentage of predictions within distance thresholds of ground truth. Metrics include 'APD-P' (strict pixel thresholds back-projected to 3D) and 'APD-M' (measured in absolute metric distances from 0.1 m to 1.0 m).

### 4.2 Main Results
- Short clips (48 frames): TrackEverything outperformed the dense all-frame tracker VDPM by more than 20% in average APD-P. Even compared to the massive D4RT model (>1B parameters trained on private data), the 61M-parameter TrackEverything achieved superior performance on subsets like ADT.
- Long sequences: Prior dense all-frame trackers (VDPM and D4RT) failed completely due to out-of-memory errors. TrackEverything ran to completion, matching or exceeding state-of-the-art sparse trackers (such as SpatialTracker-v2) despite tracking orders of magnitude more points.

### 4.3 Scaling and Computational Cost
Using long sequences from PointOdyssey, the authors analyzed behavior across varying frame counts and query point counts.
- Scaling with video length: Competing methods experienced rapid memory growth: Any4D crashed at 96 frames, SpatialTracker-v2 at 200 frames, and CoTracker3 around 600 frames. In contrast, TrackEverything kept memory below 30 GB even at 900 frames, exhibiting very mild growth.
- Scaling with query points: Increasing query points up to 10,000 kept inference latency almost flat, thanks to bypassing 4D correlation volumes.

### 4.4 Ablation Studies
- Static vs. Dynamic Separation: Decoding trajectories for all points as dynamic caused latency to surge 4.8x and peak memory 2.5x, with no change in accuracy (31.2 APD-P). This highlights the efficiency of filtering for dynamic points.
- Voxel De-Duplication: Disabling voxelization led to immediate OOM errors, proving de-duplication is the backbone of long-horizon dense tracking. A voxel size of $v=0.02$ offered the best balance between accuracy and memory.

captions.F4: Qualitative comparison with baselines on a barn scene with cows. Only one cow is visible in the first frame; a second cow enters later. First-frame dense trackers and sparse trackers fail to track the cow that appears later, whereas TrackEverything (leftmost column) densely tracks newly emerging surfaces without missing them.

sections.heading: Remaining challenges: irreversible merging risks and reliance on geometry
sections.summary: Average pooling in voxelization is irreversible, creating a risk that tracking errors permanently merge distinct surfaces. The framework also relies on external depth estimation accuracy, and open-ended exploration requires cache eviction to manage memory.
sections.details:
Despite its strengths, TrackEverything has several limitations:

- Risk of Irreversible Voxel Merging: De-duplication at window boundaries merges points via average pooling based purely on spatial proximity. If the tracker misestimates a position, two distinct physical surfaces can be permanently collapsed into a single track with no way to separate them later. (Crucial points can bypass this by running through a separate dedicated query branch).
- Reliance on External 3D Geometry: The pipeline requires depth or point clouds as input (e.g., from VGGT-$\Omega$). While modularity allows it to directly benefit from better geometry estimators, distorted point clouds directly hurt tracking accuracy.
- Memory Growth in Ever-Expanding Spaces: Token counts stay flat within a bounded room, but if a camera continuously navigates an unexplored open world, new geometry accumulates and memory gradually increases. Handling hour-long videos will require a cache eviction mechanism to prune distant past spaces.

sections.heading: Conclusion: a major step toward 3D foundation models for dynamic worlds
sections.summary: TrackEverything decouples computation from video duration by de-duplicating 3D voxels in world coordinates. Achieving dense 3D tracking on long videos under practical compute budgets paves the way for next-generation dynamic 3D foundation models.
sections.details:
This paper presented TrackEverything, a 3D tracker capable of following all visible surfaces across long videos.

Guided by the principle that computational complexity should scale with physical scene geometry rather than frame count, the method combines voxel-based de-duplication, endpoint-first static/dynamic separation, and fast 3D WAFT feature sampling. As a result, dense 3D tracking on videos exceeding 1,000 frames is made practical for the first time on a single 40 GB GPU.

For embodied AI agents in robotic manipulation and autonomous driving, persistent and compact 3D representations are a powerful asset. TrackEverything establishes foundational technology that is poised to make a substantial impact on future robotics and vision research.

sections.heading: Appendix: speeding up inference and pipeline details
sections.summary: The appendix introduces 'Early Merge'—merging static points right after the first refinement iteration to boost inference speed by ~1.8x (23.1 FPS average)—and provides detailed ablation results on long video benchmarks.
sections.details:
The appendix covers implementation details and supplementary experimental results.

### Early Merge in Initial Refinement
While voxel de-duplication normally occurs at window boundaries, an optional 'Early Merge' merges points classified as static immediately after Iteration 0 of the endpoint refiner. Because static/dynamic classification converges almost completely after a single iteration, pruning static points early has no negative impact on tracking accuracy (31.2 vs. 31.3 APD-P).
This modification increases tracker speed from an average of 12.6 FPS to 23.1 FPS (~1.8x speedup). In static-camera laboratory scenes (PStudio), it reaches a real-time rate of 41.5 FPS.

### Synthetic Benchmark Evaluation and Full History Reconstruction
TrackEverything also outperformed baselines on PointOdyssey and Dynamic Replica (Table 3), benchmarks featuring dense ground-truth 3D annotations. Furthermore, although voxelization merges active points in memory, the system records step-wise merge mapping histories and spatial offset residuals during inference. This allows it to fully reconstruct complete 3D trajectory histories $\mathbf{X}$ at original resolution for all initial points across the entire video.

captions.F5: Sliding-window and de-duplication pipeline. At the end of the top window (Window i), 46,000 tracking points are compressed down to 16,000 via voxelization by removing co-located duplicates. In the next window (Window i+1), these 16,000 retained points combine with new points generated from fresh frames, continuing tracking without redundancy.
captions.F6: Visualization of 3D WAFT projection and iterative refinement. The top row illustrates the offset between constant-velocity initialization (red) and ground truth (green). The bottom row shows how reprojections converge toward ground truth over iterations (Iter 0–2), with sampled feature patches aligning to the visually correct region.

takeaways: Treating video as geometry in a 3D world coordinate frame rather than evolving 2D pixels fundamentally eliminates redundant token buildup across time.
Separating static scene areas from moving objects and decoding expensive trajectories solely for dynamic points cuts computation by multiples without sacrificing accuracy.
Projecting 3D predicted positions onto 2D feature maps via bilinear sampling (3D WAFT) achieves high-accuracy correspondence search without memory-heavy 4D correlation volumes.
Decoupling the tracker from external geometry estimators (depth or SLAM) allows the system to seamlessly absorb improvements in hardware sensors and 3D foundation models without retraining.
limitations: Voxel merging at window boundaries is an irreversible average-pooling step; if tracking errors cause points from different surfaces to merge into the same voxel, they can never be separated.
Tracking accuracy depends directly on the geometric quality of the input 3D point cloud maps (e.g., depth estimation), degrading if geometry estimation fails heavily.
While token counts remain stable in bounded environments, memory grows linearly with explored area in open-ended navigation, making cache eviction mechanisms necessary for very long sessions.
